title: Non-Hermitian Schwinger effect in an imaginary magnetic field
abstract: We investigate a non-Hermitian Schwinger effect by analyzing a one-loop effective Lagrangian of scalar and Dirac quantum electrodynamics (QED) in the presence of a real electric field and a parallel imaginary magnetic field. We show that an imaginary magnetic field produces an additional pole family in the integrand of the proper-time representation. Unlike a real magnetic field, an imaginary magnetic field can generate a nonzero imaginary part of the effective Lagrangian even in the absence of an electric field. The interplay between the two fields leads to nontrivial phenomena, such as a cancellation mechanism between the contributions of two fields. We also point out that when the ratio of two field strengths is rational, some poles among the two families coincide, and a careful treatment of double poles is required. By further examining the complex Landau-level structure of the electric-pole contribution, we find that the field dependence of the vacuum decay rate from each Landau level exhibits a sinusoidal-like behavior, and their sum determines the overall field dependence. Our results clarify the analytic structure of the QED effective Lagrangian in imaginary magnetic backgrounds and provide a basis for investigating its relation to non-Hermitian phenomena in the QED vacuum.
summary: This work analyzes the non-Hermitian Schwinger effect in QED using an imaginary magnetic field. The authors find that this field can induce vacuum decay independently of an electric field, a phenomenon not seen with real magnetic fields. The mathematical treatment is complex, requiring careful handling of pole structures depending on the ratio of the applied fields.
main_problem: The paper investigates the non-Hermitian Schwinger effect, analyzing how vacuum instability (pair creation) is modified by the presence of an imaginary magnetic field in conjunction with a real electric field.
main_result: An imaginary magnetic field can induce vacuum decay even when no electric field is present, and the field dependence of the decay rate exhibits complex sinusoidal-like behavior depending on whether the field ratio is rational or irrational.
method: The analysis relies on calculating the one-loop effective Lagrangian using the proper-time representation, requiring careful treatment of pole structures in the integrand.
model_or_system: The system is Scalar and Dirac Quantum Electrodynamics (QED) subjected to combined real electric ($\mathbf{E}$) and imaginary magnetic ($\mathbf{B}_I$) fields.
key_observables: The imaginary part of the effective Lagrangian ($	ext{Im} L$), which determines the vacuum decay rate ($\Gamma = 2 	ext{Im} L$).
important_parameters: Electric field strength ($\mathbf{E}$), imaginary magnetic field strength ($\mathbf{B}_I$), and the ratio $\mathbf{B}_I/\mathbf{E}$ (rational vs. irrational).
main_assumptions: The calculation requires distinguishing between the irrational and rational ratios of the field strengths, as this dictates the pole structure and the need to treat double poles.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the contour prescriptions for the proper-time integral, showing how imaginary fields shift poles onto the real axis, and plot the vacuum decay rate ($\Gamma$) in the $(	ext{E}, 	ext{B})$ and $(	ext{E}, 	ext{BI})$ planes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the general framework for the non-Hermitian Schwinger effect, then detailing the calculation of $	ext{Im} L$ by separating the analysis into the irrational and rational field ratio regimes, and finally deriving the complex Landau-level contributions.
why_interesting: The study of non-Hermitian Hamiltonians and effective Lagrangians is highly relevant to open quantum systems and quantum optics, as non-Hermiticity naturally arises when coupling to an environment or when considering decay processes.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Contour prescription for the proper-time integral. (a) For a real magnetic field, the electric E poles lie on the real axis and contribute to the imaginary part of effective Lagrangian through the deformed integration contour, while the magnetic B poles remain on the imaginary axis. (b) After the analytic continuation B →iBI, the magnetic BI poles move onto the real axis and also contribute to the imaginary part.

FIG. 3. The imaginary part of the effective Lagrangian for (a) scalar and (b) Dirac QED as a function of the imaginary (left) and real (right) magnetic fields at fixed |eE|/m2 = 0.5 (blue) and 1 (red). In the imaginary-field region, the solid lines show the full result, including both E- and BI-pole contributions, while the dotted lines show the E-pole contribution alone. A real magnetic field suppresses the scalar result and enhances the Dirac result, whereas the imaginary-field region exhibits nonmonotonic and, for Dirac QED, sign-changing behavior.

FIG. 2. The imaginary part of the effective Lagrangian, Γ = 2ImL, for scalar and Dirac QED as functions of the electric and magnetic fields: (a) real magnetic field B and (b) imaginary magnetic field BI.

FIG. 4. The imaginary part of the effective Lagrangian for scalar and Dirac QED along the line of |eE| = |eBI|. The scalar result is positive and increases with the field strength, whereas the Dirac result is negative and satisfies ΓDirac = −2Γscalar.

FIG. 5. Electric-pole (left), imaginary-magnetic-pole (middle), and total (right) contributions to the imaginary part of the effective Lagrangian in scalar QED as functions of the imaginary magnetic field strength |eBI|/m2 at fixed |eE|/m2 = 1. The upper, middle, and lower rows correspond to truncation orders nmax(kmax) = 1, 2, and 3, respectively.
